title: Ugh I love a good historical drama! +10 points to whoever can tell me...
transcript: I am a little embarrassed to say that I actually knew nothing about Mary Todd Lincoln going into omarie. And in the same way that Hamilton brought Alexander Hamilton to the public consciousness, I'm really hoping the same happens with omarie and Mary Todd Lincoln, because after seeing the show, I feel like I've Learned so much about this woman that our history classes really don't teach us. I really only knew her as Abraham Lincoln's wife, and I had no idea that she actually got her start as a cabaret performer and had dreams of becoming a star. But writer and star Kola Scola also does not shy away from showing some of Mary's flaws at this play. Also depicts her struggles with alcoholism and her abrasive personality. I also think Colascola was born to play Mary, because there is a portrait of her in it, the lobby of the theater, and it looks exactly like Colascola. Like, if you told me that was actually Colascola, I would believe you. It is so clear that Cole put so much care and research into making sure that they were telling Mary's story as authentically and true to life as possible. And not just Mary. I feel like I also Learned a ton about Abraham Lincoln, who I didn't realize was basically our country's first gay president. This feels so monumental, and I'm really surprised that more history books don't talk about it. Although, come to think of it, erasing the Contributions of gay people to our country's history does feel very on brand. But I think perhaps the most surprising revelation in this whole play is just how prolific Mary was in the music industry. The show ends with a faithful recreation of one of her mad cat medleys, in which she matches up a bunch of songs, many of which haven't even been recorded yet. The songs like Copacabana, which I assumed was originated by Barry Manilow, because his recorded version is the one that I'm most familiar with. That song is apparently actually a cover and can be traced back to Mary's cabaret act. And so I really hope that through the show, audiences cannot only learn about this woman that history has largely forgotten, but that she can finally get the credit that she deserves for her contributions to art and culture. So thank you, Cole Escola, for telling Mary's story. She may have been difficult, but boy, can she sing.
